candidate.blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential — monitor vital signs, recognize abnormal findings and follow up on changes, detailed content pp. 40-42.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — temperature/vital-sign interpretation
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize a markedly elevated adult oral temperature as fever and assess associated symptoms and clinical context rather than treating the value as normal, hypothermic, or insignificant.

options.A: It is within the expected adult oral-temperature range and requires no illness assessment unless hypotension also develops.
options.B: It indicates hypothermia and should prompt warming measures before evaluating other possible causes.
options.C: It is only mildly elevated and below the usual fever range, so no additional assessment is needed unless it rises further.
options.D: It represents fever and warrants assessment of the client's symptoms and clinical context to identify a possible underlying cause.

candidate.rationale: MedlinePlus states that a high body temperature is fever and that an adult probably has a fever when oral temperature is above about 99°F to 99.5°F (37.2°C to 37.5°C), depending on time of day. It also notes that a temperature more than 1°F to 1.5°F above a person's normal temperature is fever and that fever can accompany many illnesses. An oral temperature of 39.2°C (102.6°F) is therefore clearly febrile and should be interpreted with the client's symptoms and clinical context. A, B, and C misclassify the temperature or delay appropriate assessment.
candidate.source_claim_supported: High temperature is fever; adult oral temperatures well above normal, including 39.2°C, are febrile and should be interpreted in clinical context because fever may reflect infection or other illness.
candidate.source_locator: Temperature measurement — Normal Results and What Abnormal Results Mean; Fever — adult oral fever definition and Considerations.
candidate.source_version_date: Temperature measurement reviewed January 14, 2026; current MedlinePlus fever guidance
candidate.stem: An adult client's oral temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F). How should the nurse interpret this finding?
